content: 1. Once a patient is diagnosed and enrolled in chronic care, follow-up visits must be systematically scheduled and planned. Delaying care until symptoms or preventable complications arise is both costly and inefficient. 2. Individuals living with HIV require care that anticipates their needs at various stages of the care continuum. Compared to acute care models, planned chronic care models offer opportunities for prevention, early identification of issues, and timely intervention. 3. Effective chronic care for people living with HIV necessitates comprehensive support from their communities and healthcare teams to ensure they remain engaged in care, adhere to treatment, and manage stigma. 4. People living with HIV and their families must be educated about HIV infection, the potential side effects of medications, and supported in adhering to treatment regimens. 5. Healthcare teams play a critical role in connecting individuals living with HIV to community-level interventions, resources, and support systems. 6. Maintaining a robust system to track patient information at healthcare facilities is essential for ensuring continuity of chronic care. A patient registry serves as a tool for follow-up reminders, identifying patient needs, planning care, monitoring treatment responses, and assessing outcomes for both individuals and the broader treatment cohort. 7. Information systems can be paper-based or electronic, depending on the local context. Programs should develop systematic strategies for collecting and aggregating key data to improve patient management and ensure high-quality care. 8. A strong patient information system is also vital for high-quality monitoring and evaluation of programs, as well as for managing medical supply chains. 9. When effective operational solutions, such as successful service delivery models and care processes, are identified, programs should consider scaling up these models to enhance care delivery. 10. Chronic care requires the integration and linkage of related services to ensure comprehensive and consistent patient management over time. This includes providing related services in single settings, establishing systems for information sharing, and ensuring effective referrals across settings and providers. 11. Integrating and linking services can reduce missed opportunities for initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), enhance long-term adherence support, and optimize patient retention in care. 12. Collaboration among HIV, sexual and reproductive health, maternal and child health, tuberculosis (TB), and drug dependence programs is essential for successfully implementing ART and related services at various levels of the healthcare system. 13. Key considerations include mobilizing and allocating resources, training and supervising healthcare workers, procuring and managing medical supplies, and conducting monitoring and evaluation. 14. In maternal and child health settings, ART should be initiated and maintained for eligible pregnant and postpartum women and infants, with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART where appropriate. 15. Maternal and child health clinics should either provide ART directly or ensure easy access through linked clinics. In generalized epidemic settings, a phased approach to transforming maternal and child health settings into ART sites may be considered, prioritizing facilities with the highest HIV burden. 16. A significant challenge is ensuring the continuation of ART beyond the mother-to-child transmission risk period. Not all maternal and child health settings may have the capacity to provide long-term HIV care and treatment for women, their partners, and infants. 17. In settings with a high burden of HIV and TB, ART should be initiated for individuals living with HIV in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. 18. TB treatment should be initiated first, followed by ART as soon as possible within the first eight weeks of starting TB treatment. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is also recommended for all TB patients with HIV. 19. Offering ART and TB treatment at a single site can improve access and adherence by providing a continuum of care from HIV testing to co-treatment for HIV and TB. 20. Implementing TB infection control measures in HIV care settings is crucial to minimize the risk of nosocomial transmission of TB. 21. ART should be initiated and maintained in eligible individuals living with HIV at care settings where opioid substitution therapy (OST) is provided. However, enrollment in OST should not be a prerequisite for initiating or maintaining ART. 22. Efforts should be made to ensure ART is available as part of prison health services and to maintain continuity of HIV care and ART when individuals transition from incarceration to the community. 23. People who inject drugs are a marginalized population with limited access to healthcare services. Integrating opioid substitution therapy with HIV treatment can improve ART outcomes for this population. 24. ART outcomes improve among people living with HIV who inject drugs and access opioid substitution therapy. However, ART should be accessible regardless of OST enrollment. 25. Programs should prioritize expanding ART access and reducing barriers, such as long waiting times and transportation costs, to improve retention in care for pregnant and breastfeeding women, as well as other key populations.
